The paper was published in 2007 in Mathematical Methods in the Applied Sciences.
The layered scatterer consists of n homogeneous layers with constant material parameters in each layer.
The scatterer's core can be perfect conducting, impedance, or dielectric.
The primary spherical electric field generated by a magnetic dipole is normalized to reduce to a plane wave at infinity.
The total field in the dipole's layer is the sum of the primary and secondary fields.
Transmission boundary conditions ensure continuity of tangential electric fields and their curls across layer interfaces.
The secondary field satisfies the Silver–Müller radiation condition at infinity.
Reciprocity theorem relates total electric fields at two dipole locations inside the scatterer involving spherical Hankel functions.
General scattering theorems relate total, primary, and secondary electric fields with their far-field patterns.
The optical theorem relates the scattering cross-section to the secondary electric field at the dipole location inside the scatterer.
Mixed scattering theorems connect spherical and plane wave excitations and are important for inverse scattering.
Numerical implementation includes computation of the extinction cross-section of a two-layered sphere.
The primary electric far-field pattern has no radial components.
The layered scatterer is modeled as a compact subset of R3 with C2 smooth boundaries.
The paper extends previous results for exterior dipole excitation to interior dipole excitation.
The study uses vector Green's second theorem and Sommerfeld's integral method in proofs.
The scattering cross-section is defined as the average power radiated in the far-field due to a dipole inside a layer.
The paper provides formulas for absorption cross-section for lossy dielectric cores.
The results serve as Green's functions for integral equation formulations in layered media.
Applications include medical hyperthermia, biotelemetry, antenna design, and optical waveguide scattering.
